```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)

orders <- read_csv("data/orders.csv")
order_items <- read_csv("data/order_items.csv")
products <- read_csv("data/products.csv")
sellers <- read_csv("data/sellers.csv")

orders_clean <- orders |>
  filter(order_status == "delivered") |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days)) |>
  mutate(
    delivery_status = if_else(
      delivery_days <= estimated_days,
      "On Time",
      "Late"
    )
  )

supply_chain_data <- orders_clean |>
  left_join(order_items, by = "order_id") |>
  left_join(sellers, by = "seller_id") |>
  left_join(products, by = "product_id") |>
  mutate(
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price
  )
```

The marketplace depends on many independent sellers to fulfill customer orders.

As the business grows, management needs to know whether the seller groups handling the most marketplace activity are also delivering reliably and at a reasonable logistics cost.

The exploration focuses on this question:

**Which seller groups are helping the marketplace scale efficiently, and which ones may need more attention?**

## Marketplace benchmark

Before comparing seller groups, I first calculated overall marketplace performance.

```{r}
overall_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100
  )

overall_performance
```

The marketplace contains **`r overall_performance$total_items` items**.

Average delivery time is **`r round(overall_performance$average_delivery_days, 1)` days**, average freight cost is **`r round(overall_performance$average_freight_cost, 1)`**, and the overall on-time delivery rate is **`r round(overall_performance$on_time_rate, 1)`%**.

These values act as the benchmark for the comparisons that follow.

```{r}
state_names <- tibble(
  seller_state = c(
    "SP", "MG", "PR", "RJ",
    "SC", "RS", "DF", "BA"
  ),
  seller_name = c(
    "São Paulo",
    "Minas Gerais",
    "Paraná",
    "Rio de Janeiro",
    "Santa Catarina",
    "Rio Grande do Sul",
    "Federal District",
    "Bahia"
  )
)

seller_state_performance <- supply_chain_data |>
  group_by(seller_state) |>
  summarise(
    total_items = n(),
    average_delivery_days = mean(delivery_days),
    average_freight_cost = mean(freight_value),
    average_freight_ratio = mean(freight_ratio, na.rm = TRUE),
    on_time_rate = mean(delivery_status == "On Time") * 100,
    average_product_weight = mean(product_weight_g, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state")

top_8_states <- seller_state_performance |>
  head(8)

largest_state <- top_8_states |>
  arrange(desc(total_items)) |>
  head(1)

largest_state_share <-
  largest_state$total_items /
  overall_performance$total_items * 100
```

## 1. Which seller groups matter most — and are they reliable?

Marketplace scale matters because performance problems in a large seller group can affect far more orders than the same problem in a small seller group.

### 1a. Which states combine marketplace scale with delivery performance?

The first chart combines item volume, on-time delivery performance, and average freight cost.

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = total_items,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = average_freight_cost,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "High marketplace volume does not always mean stronger fulfillment",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents average freight cost",
    x = "Number of Items",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Average Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r largest_state$seller_name`** handles **`r largest_state$total_items` items**, representing about **`r round(largest_state_share, 1)`%** of marketplace activity.

Its scale makes its delivery performance especially important because even a small change can affect a large number of orders.

### 1b. Which major seller states are above or below the delivery benchmark?

To make the delivery difference easier to see, I compared each major seller state directly with the overall marketplace on-time rate.

```{r}
delivery_comparison <- top_8_states |>
  mutate(
    difference_from_average =
      on_time_rate - overall_performance$on_time_rate
  )

best_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(desc(difference_from_average)) |>
  head(1)

weakest_delivery_state <- delivery_comparison |>
  arrange(difference_from_average) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
ggplot(
  delivery_comparison,
  aes(
    x = difference_from_average,
    y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
  )
) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 0,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_segment(
    aes(
      x = 0,
      xend = difference_from_average,
      y = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average),
      yend = reorder(seller_name, difference_from_average)
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(color = difference_from_average > 0),
    size = 4
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Major seller states fall on both sides of the delivery benchmark",
    subtitle = "Difference from the overall marketplace on-time rate",
    x = "Percentage Points Above or Below Marketplace Average",
    y = "Seller State",
    color = "Above Average"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r best_delivery_state$seller_name`** performs the strongest relative to the marketplace benchmark, while **`r weakest_delivery_state$seller_name`** has the weakest performance among the eight largest seller states.

The important point is that an underperforming seller state becomes more important when it also handles a large amount of marketplace activity.

## 2. Which seller groups show the biggest operational concern?

Delivery performance and freight burden should not be judged separately.

A seller group with strong delivery and low freight burden looks very different from one with weaker delivery and high freight cost relative to product value.

```{r}
ggplot(
  top_8_states,
  aes(
    x = average_freight_ratio,
    y = on_time_rate,
    size = total_items,
    color = seller_name
  )
) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = overall_performance$average_freight_ratio,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = overall_performance$on_time_rate,
    linetype = "dashed"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Seller states face different combinations of freight burden and delivery performance",
    subtitle = "Bubble size represents marketplace item volume",
    x = "Average Freight-to-Price Ratio",
    y = "On-Time Delivery Rate (%)",
    color = "Seller State",
    size = "Number of Items"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** The chart separates the major seller states into different operating positions.

Seller groups above the horizontal benchmark have stronger delivery performance, while seller groups to the right of the vertical benchmark carry a higher freight burden.

The groups that fall below the delivery benchmark while also sitting above the freight benchmark deserve the closest management attention.

However, higher freight cost may not always be caused by poor seller performance.

The next step is to check whether the products being shipped help explain the difference.

## 3. Are higher logistics costs caused by the seller — or by what they ship?

Product characteristics can affect freight cost.

In particular, heavier products would normally be expected to cost more to transport.

### 3a. Does product weight help explain freight cost?

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Heavier products generally cost more to ship",
    subtitle = "Relationship between product weight and freight cost",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** Freight cost generally increases as product weight increases.

This means higher freight cost does not automatically mean a seller group is inefficient.

Part of the cost difference may simply come from the types of products being shipped.

### 3b. Does the relationship change across major seller states?

If product weight explained freight cost in exactly the same way everywhere, the relationship should look similar across seller states.

I therefore compared the four highest-volume states separately.

```{r}
top_4_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(4)

top_4_state_names <- top_4_states$seller_name
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_4_state_names) |>
  filter(!is.na(product_weight_g)) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = product_weight_g,
      y = freight_value
    )
  ) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ seller_name) +
  labs(
    title = "Freight patterns still differ across the largest seller states",
    subtitle = "Product weight and freight cost for the four highest-volume states",
    x = "Product Weight (grams)",
    y = "Freight Cost"
  ) +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** The four largest seller states all show higher freight costs as product weight increases, but the patterns are not identical.

Product weight therefore explains part of the freight difference, but seller location and other fulfillment factors may also matter.

## 4. Are averages hiding bigger cost problems?

Average freight cost is useful, but it can hide unusually expensive shipments.

To look beyond the average, I compared the full freight-cost distributions of the five largest seller states.

```{r}
top_5_states <- top_8_states |>
  head(5)

top_5_state_names <- top_5_states$seller_name

highest_freight_state <- top_5_states |>
  arrange(desc(average_freight_cost)) |>
  head(1)
```

```{r}
supply_chain_data |>
  left_join(state_names, by = "seller_state") |>
  filter(seller_name %in% top_5_state_names) |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = seller_name,
      y = freight_value,
      fill = seller_name
    )
  ) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_boxplot(
    width = 0.12,
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Average freight cost hides large differences between shipments",
    subtitle = "Freight-cost distributions for the five largest seller states",
    x = "Seller State",
    y = "Freight Cost",
    fill = "Seller State"
  ) +
  guides(fill = "none") +
  theme_light()
```

**What this shows:** **`r highest_freight_state$seller_name`** has the highest average freight cost among the five largest seller states at about **`r round(highest_freight_state$average_freight_cost, 1)`**.

The distribution also shows that some seller groups contain shipments that are much more expensive than most of their orders.

Those shipments would be difficult to notice if management looked only at average freight cost.

## What does this mean for management?

The exploration shows that seller performance should not be judged using only volume, delivery performance, or freight cost by itself.

High-volume seller groups matter more because even small improvements can affect a large number of marketplace orders.

At the same time, higher freight costs should not automatically be treated as seller inefficiency because heavier products naturally cost more to ship.

Management should therefore focus most closely on seller groups that combine:

- high marketplace volume,
- delivery performance below the marketplace benchmark,
- freight burden above the marketplace benchmark, and
- freight costs that cannot be fully explained by the products being shipped.

The biggest opportunity is to identify places where a small operational improvement could have a large effect on marketplace growth.
